## Summary

Build fixed no-argument core schemas once and return a fresh shallow copy from the existing direct type handlers. title: Construct builtin scalar union schemas directly
body:
Depends on #14141, based on `codex/scalar-schema-fast-paths` (merged at e68c354f9). This stacks direct union construction on top of the scalar entry-point fast paths. Alternative to the union cache in #14131; that PR uses an earlier base.

Repeated flat unions currently pass every member through general schema generation. For unions composed exclusively of exact types accepted by `_is_simple_schema_type` (including its interpreter-specific exclusions), construct the known union/nullable dictionary shape directly using fresh member schemas from the existing handlers. Member order is preserved. Configured `json_encoders` and unsupported shapes use normal union generation. Field metadata, validators, serializers, and discriminator handling remain in their normal processing paths.

This uses no union cache, cache key, eviction, or shared union schemas. The small schema-shape assumption is explicit in the construction code and tested against the general union generator for all ordered two- and three-member combinations of the supported types. Tests reject fallback to the general path. For `re.Pattern` and `ZoneInfo`, whose handlers create fresh callbacks, equivalence is checked through JSON Schema, validation, and serialization.

Validation after reusing `_is_simple_schema_type`: 4,527 union/scalar tests passed, 12 skipped, 4 xfailed on CPython; 1,175 direct-union/scalar-fast-path tests passed on PyPy. Pyright and all pre-commit checks passed.

Earlier validation after merging the new base: 324 targeted union/scalar cases passed, 12 skipped. Full suite: 13,643 passed, 491 skipped, 36 xfailed. Pyright passed; pre-commit checks passed.

## Historical profiling and performance

The results below predate the move onto #14141. They compare the earlier variants against 375c241; they do not measure the incremental benefit over the current scalar-fast-path base. Current CodSpeed runs will compare against #14141.

Profiling identified repeated eligibility scans in both approaches. The cache checks exact member identity without per-member `id()`/dictionary lookups. Direct construction records nullability during eligibility checking and constructs choices only after all members qualify, preserving the unsupported-member fallback path.

The union-specific work now runs in dedicated methods. Keeping it inside `_generate_schema_inner` had enlarged the general dispatcher's frame even for plain scalar fields. Method extraction restores that dispatcher to the base's 4 locals and 992 bytecode bytes (previously 7 locals/1212 bytes for the cache and 9 locals/1534 bytes for direct construction).

Matched final timings for rebuilding 100-field models, in milliseconds (lower is better):

| Field shape | Shared base | Cache (#14131) | Direct (#14138) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `str` control | 0.8896 | 0.8966 | 0.8833 |
| `int \| str` | 1.7361 | 1.4619 | 1.4375 |

In the same experiment, the cache before extraction took 0.9392 ms for the scalar control, so its slowdown reproduced and was largely removed by extraction. The direct version's earlier scalar slowdown did not reproduce in this run: it took 0.8890 ms before extraction. Remaining control differences are under 1%; neither option has an established scalar speedup.

All variants used the same Python 3.14.7 interpreter and pydantic-core 2.50.0 build, fixed `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`, and four fresh interpreter runs per variant interleaved in forward/reverse order. Each model had eight warmups, then seven batches of 150 rebuilds. Values are medians of process medians. The shared base is `375c241b0c619f6984f3c08432daaee2f6d5b5fc`.

These measurements concern schema rebuilding, not string-value validation or overall SDK/import throughput. title: Cache the generated core schema of pure field annotations
body:
## Change Summary

The same field annotation (e.g. `str | None`) is typically repeated across many fields and models — an SDK with hundreds of models uses a handful of annotation shapes thousands of times — and every occurrence went through the full schema generation pipeline, producing structurally identical schema dicts.

This PR caches the generated core schema for **pure** annotations: those composed only of immutable C leaf types (`str`, `int`, `datetime`, …) and of typing constructs over them (unions/optionals, literals of primitive values, builtin containers). For these, the generated schema is provably identical every time:

- no custom `__get_pydantic_core_schema__` / `__get_pydantic_json_schema__` hook can be attached to any type involved (C types are immutable, and generic aliases don't proxy dunder access),
- no configuration read during generation can affect the result — the one exception, the deprecated `json_encoders` setting, bypasses the cache,
- no generation context (namespaces, typevar maps, reference definitions) is involved: pure annotations contain no forward references, type variables or referenceable types.

The following edge cases are covered by unit tests:

- **Order sensitivity**: `Union[int, str]` and `Union[str, int]` (and literal permutations) compare and hash equal, but their schemas differ, so the cache key is a canonical nested-tuple key that preserves argument order — the annotation objects themselves would be unsound keys.
- **No shared mutable state**: cache hits return a deep copy, and the stored schema is a pristine copy taken before any downstream mutation, so `Model.__pydantic_core_schema__` objects of different models never alias each other.

- **Tuple shapes and aliases**: schema generation and cache keys share tuple-argument normalization, distinguishing arbitrary-length tuples from fixed empty tuples, including Python 3.10 spelling differences. Bare deprecated aliases reuse schema dispatch's existing alias map.
- **Memory retention**: the cache admits at most 512 entries and 8 KiB of combined literal-value payload per annotation, including nested literals. Oversized annotations generate normally without caching. The payload bound excludes schema and key-container overhead; PyPy uses conservative size estimates.

Measured (release build, fresh interpreter, interleaved A/B against main):

- synthetic 600 models × 3 `Optional[str]` fields: ~15% off model-definition time on top of #13540/#13541 (~25–30% for the three PRs combined)
- real world: `import mcp` (mcp 2.0.0, 643 models): per-module `-X importtime` self-time of the model-defining modules drops 202ms → 180ms with all three PRs; whole-import wall time −20 to −30ms

* [x] Unit tests for the changes exist

title: Warn when `validate_call` drops undeclared unpacked `TypedDict` kwargs (#14203)

### Summary

Fixes #14203.

When using `@validate_call` with `**kwargs: Unpack[TD]`, undeclared keyword arguments were previously dropped silently due to `TypedDict`'s default `extra='ignore'`. This caused misspelled options or unrecognized parameters to run unnoticed with default values.

This PR adds a `PydanticDroppedUnpackedKwargWarning` (subclass of `UserWarning`) emitted when `validate_call` drops undeclared kwargs from an unpacked `TypedDict`, warning users that these keys were dropped and will raise a `ValidationError` in V3.

==== Changes====
- Added `PydanticDroppedUnpackedKwargWarning` in `pydantic/warnings.py`.
- Wrapped unpacked `TypedDict` kwargs schema with a validator in `_arguments_schema` to detect dropped keys and emit the warning with correct caller stack level.
- Added tests in `tests/test_validate_call.py` covering single/multiple dropped arguments, clean calls without warnings, and async functions.

title: perf: fast paths for scalar and container schema generation
body:
## Summary

This PR introduces a series of targeted fast paths in the core schema generation pipeline
(`_generate_schema.py` and `json_schema.py`) to reduce per-field overhead during model
construction. The changes are strictly additive: all existing behaviour is preserved, with
each fast path guarded by a cheap runtime check before activating.

The work was developed against `upstream/main` and rebased cleanly after the recent
annotation-fast-path landed in #14149 (by @alexmojaki). Where both implementations
overlapped, the upstream version was preferred and our changes were layered on top.

---

## Changes

### `pydantic/_internal/_generate_schema.py`

#### 1. Fast path for builtin scalar types in `_generate_schema_inner`

For the six core scalar types (`int`, `str`, `float`, `bool`, `bytes`, `NoneType`) the
function now returns immediately using a `frozenset` lookup table, bypassing the full
annotation-dispatch machinery. This is the hottest path for typical models.

```python
# Before: full dispatch for every type
# After: O(1) lookup for scalars
_SIMPLE_SCHEMA_TYPES: frozenset[type] = frozenset({int, str, float, bool, bytes, type(None)})
```

#### 2. Fast path for fields without annotations (`_extract_json_schema_info_from_field_info`)

When a field carries no metadata and `json_schema_extra` is `None`, the function returns
early before constructing the handler chain. This eliminates handler-chain allocation on
the majority of fields in typical models.

#### 3. Fast path for generic containers with simple inner types

`list[int]`, `dict[str, float]`, `list[str]`, etc. now skip the full generic
unwrap/repack cycle when all inner types are scalars, reducing the call depth for the
most common parameterised generics.

#### 4. Regression fix: JSON serializers preserved in discriminated-union fast path

The scalar fast path could silently discard `model_config`-level `json_encoders` when
applied inside a discriminated union. The serialization assembly step is now always
executed after the schema is built, regardless of which path was taken.

A regression test covering this case was added to
`tests/types/unions/test_discriminated_union.py`.

### `pydantic/json_schema.py`

#### 5. Skip empty handler chains in JSON schema generation

When the list of JSON schema handlers is empty the iteration loop is now short-circuited.
This reduces per-field overhead during `model_json_schema()` calls on large models with
many plain fields.

---

## Benchmark Results

Run locally on **Python 3.13 / Windows x64** with `pytest-benchmark 5.1.0`,
`--benchmark-warmup=on`, `--override-ini="addopts="` (disabling the default
`--benchmark-disable` set in `pyproject.toml`).

The benchmark tests `test_stdlib_type_schema_generation` and
`test_pydantic_custom_types_schema_generation` were enabled by temporarily removing the
`@pytest.mark.skip` decorators and restored before this PR.

## Change Summary

In `BaseModel.__eq__`, an early fast-path check `self.__dict__ == other.__dict__` is performed to avoid filtering dictionaries when instances have identical `__dict__`.

## Change Summary

**Stacked on #13542** (targets that branch; will be retargeted to `main` once it merges — only the last commit is new).

#13542 caches the *inner schema* of repeated pure annotations, but each field still pays for annotation evaluation, `FieldInfo` construction, and the per-field schema scaffolding around the cached part. This PR collapses that remaining pipeline for the most common kind of field — a pure annotation with no metadata and at most a simple immutable default (`str | None = None`, `int`, `Literal['a', 'b'] = 'a'`, …):

- **`FieldInfo` templates**: `collect_model_fields()` copies a cached template instead of re-running `inspect_annotation` + `FieldInfo` construction for every occurrence of the same `(annotation, default)` pair. The actual annotation/default objects are set on each copy, so equal-but-distinct spellings (`Union[int, str]` vs `Union[str, int]`) are preserved on `model_fields`, and instances are never shared between models.
- **Complete field-node cache**: `_generate_md_field_schema()` caches the whole `model-field` node (inner schema, default wrapper, metadata). title: Replace `impl_py_gc_traverse!` with a `#[derive(PyGcTraverse)]` macro traversing all fields
body:
Second approach to address #13625.

## What this does

Replaces the `impl_py_gc_traverse!` macro (and most hand-written `PyGcTraverse` impls) with a `#[derive(PyGcTraverse)]` proc macro, implemented in a new `pydantic-core-derive` workspace crate. The derive traverses **every** field by default:

- A field whose type doesn't implement `PyGcTraverse` is a **compile error**, forcing an explicit decision: derive on that type, add a no-op impl for plain data, or mark the field `#[py_gc(skip)]`.
- Skips are explicit, greppable, and reviewable. The entire codebase ends up with exactly **two**, both commented: the partially-uninitialized `RecursionStack::Array` buffer and `GenericIterator::JsonArray` (JSON data can't hold Python references).
- `py_gc.rs` gains no-op impls for primitives and plain external types (jiter/speedate/regex), plus container impls (`AHashSet`, `OnceLock`, `SmallVec`, 2-tuples).

Nice consequences of the migration:

- The hand-written 50-variant `CombinedSerializer` match ("implemented by hand because `enum_dispatch` fails") is now a derive.
- `EnumValidator<T>`'s four per-instantiation macro calls collapse into one generic derive.
- ~270 lines net deleted.

## Bugs this found and fixed

Migrating exposed real, previously-unknown leaks — every field the derive newly traverses was reviewed:

1. **`GeneralFieldsSerializer.extra_serializer`** was not traversed: serializer functions in `extras_schema` leaked (also caught by #13626's check; not covered by #13624). Fixed automatically by the derive.
2. **`StrConstrainedValidator`'s compiled pattern**: with `regex_engine='python-re'`, the validator holds a `Py<PyAny>` compiled pattern (`RegexEngine::PythonRe`) that was never reported to the GC. Fixed automatically by the derive.

## One trap worth reviewing closely

`DefinitionRefValidator`/`DefinitionRefSerializer` previously had deliberately *empty* traverse lists — they are the cycle-breakers for recursive schemas. Deriving all fields made them traverse `DefinitionRef<T>`, whose (previously unreachable) manual impl recursed into the definition target → infinite recursion → segfault on recursive schemas.

The fix makes `DefinitionRef<T>`'s traversal an explicit documented no-op: it is sound because every definition's content is already traversed through the `Definitions` container held by the top-level `SchemaValidator`/`SchemaSerializer`, and it removes the landmine for any future struct holding a `DefinitionRef`.

## Validation

- pydantic-core suite: 5616 passed (including `test_garbage_collection.py`), pydantic suite: 7930 passed.
- The `gc.get_referents()` completeness check (from #13626) passes for all five known leak scenarios: the three #13621 edges, `extra_serializer`, and the `python-re` pattern.
- `cargo clippy` clean (lib, tests, and the derive crate).

## Notes

- The derive crate is a path dependency; if pydantic-core is still published to crates.io, the crate needs publishing too (version is kept in lockstep) — happy to adjust.
- `/derive` is added to the sdist `include` list.
- Once PyO3/pyo3#5663 lands upstream, this crate can likely be deleted in favor of the official mechanism.

  • Fixed a regression in the B-Z division algorithm.

  • Upgrade to rand v0.10 and/or v0.9, and split rand_core.
    • The former rand feature is now split into multiple features, rand_0_9, rand_core_0_9, rand_0_10, and rand_core_0_10, depending on the version and feature set you need.

## Change Summary

Extracted from maxisbey/pydantic#16.

When a field is missing from the input and its default is used, the field name was cloned into a new `String` on every validation, only to be used as the error location if validating the default fails. It is now passed as a `&str` and only converted on the error path.

## Change Summary

Stacked on #14171 (only the last two commits are new). Extracted from maxisbey/pydantic#16:

- Skip the include/exclude filter logic (and hashing the key) when there is nothing to filter by, which is what the filter logic concludes anyway. This applies to model fields, dict entries and computed fields.

title: Improve performance of type inference during serialization
body:
## Change Summary

Stacked on #14172 (only the last two commits are new). Extracted from maxisbey/pydantic#16, for values whose type is inferred during serialization (e.g. `Any`, `dict[str, Any]`):

- Skip the recursion guard for `None`, `bool`, `int` and `str` values: they can't be part of a reference cycle, so only the depth limit is checked for them. title: Improve performance of model serialization
body:
## Change Summary

Three changes to the fields serializer used by models (and dataclasses/typed dicts for the last two), extracted from maxisbey/pydantic#16:

- Avoid looking up `__dict__` twice when serializing models outside of unions (a `hasattr()` check followed by a `getattr()`).
- Match `__dict__` keys to fields by identity: keys are usually the same `str` objects as the field names of the schema, in schema order. Fields are now stored in schema order, and a key is first compared with the next expected field name before falling back to a lookup by name.
- Only set the current field name for fields that are actually serialized (the exclusion checks don't use it).

Benchmarks (release builds, CPython 3.14, macOS arm64, each commit compared to the previous one):

| Case | `__dict__` | identity | field name |
|---|---|---|---|
| `model_dump()`, list of 100 small models | -15% | -11% | ~ |
| `model_dump_json()`, list of 100 small models | -15% | -12% | ~ |
| `model_dump()`, 20 fields | -2% | -21% | ~ |
| `model_dump()`, 3 fields | -2.5..-7% | -8% | ~ |
| `model_dump(exclude_none=True)`, 15/20 fields `None` | | | -4% |

title: Reject a minus sign after leading zeros when parsing integers from strings
body:
## Change Summary

In lax mode, a minus sign following leading zeros was accepted when parsing integers from strings, and interpreted as a unary minus:

```python
from pydantic import TypeAdapter

ta = TypeAdapter(int)

ta.validate_python('0-1')
#> before: -1
#> after: ValidationError: Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer
TypeAdapter(dict[int, int]).validate_json('{"00-5": 1}')
#> before: {-5: 1}
#> after: ValidationError
```

`strip_leading_zeros()` still accepted `-`, a leftover from before `clean_int_str()` handled the sign itself. Valid negative values (e.g. `'-0001'`) are unaffected. This also matches Python, where `int('0-1')` raises.
